claim: Class I ventral posterior dendritic arborisation (c1vpda) proprioceptive sensory neurons respond to contractions in the Drosophila larval body wall during crawling.
source: Class I ventral posterior dendritic arborisation (c1vpda) proprioceptive sensory neurons respond to contractions in the Drosophila larval body wall during crawling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Heckscher et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2007; Song et al., 2007; Vaadia et al., 2019).

claim: c1vpda dendritic branches run along the direction of contraction.
source: Their dendritic branches run along the direction of contraction, possibly a functional requirement to maximise membrane curvature during crawling contractions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the morphological analysis and functional imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: The orientation of c1vpda dendritic branches along the direction of contraction is possibly a functional requirement to maximise membrane curvature during crawling contractions.
source: Their dendritic branches run along the direction of contraction, possibly a functional requirement to maximise membrane curvature during crawling contractions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the abstract, later supported by modeling and experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The molecular machinery of dendritic patterning in c1vpda has been extensively studied.
source: Although the molecular machinery of dendritic patterning in c1vpda has been extensively studied, the process leading to the precise elaboration of their comb-like shapes remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior research in the field.

claim: The process leading to the precise elaboration of c1vpda comb-like shapes remains elusive.
source: Although the molecular machinery of dendritic patterning in c1vpda has been extensively studied, the process leading to the precise elaboration of their comb-like shapes remains elusive.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Long-term, non-invasive, in vivo time-lapse imaging of c1vpda embryonic and larval morphogenesis reveals a sequence of differentiation stages.
source: Here, to link dendrite shape with its proprioceptive role, we performed long-term, non-invasive, in vivo time-lapse imaging of c1vpda embryonic and larval morphogenesis to reveal a sequence of differentiation stages.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Distinct sequential phases of stochastic growth and retraction achieve efficient dendritic trees both in terms of wire and function.
source: We combined computer models and dendritic branch dynamics tracking to propose that distinct sequential phases of stochastic growth and retraction achieve efficient dendritic trees both in terms of wire and function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by computational modeling and experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Dendrite growth balances structure–function requirements.
source: Our study shows how dendrite growth balances structure–function requirements, shedding new light on general principles of self-organisation in functionally specialised dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, supported by the data on wire optimization and functional curvature.

claim: The coupling of class type-specific dendrite geometry with various ion channels provides the substrate for signal processing and integration in dendrites.
source: In the past, technological and conceptual advances have allowed exciting discoveries on how the coupling of class type-specific dendrite geometry with various ion channels provide the substrate for signal processing and integration in dendrites (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1996; van Elburg and van Ooyen, 2010; Gabbiani et al., 2002; London and Häusser, 2005; Branco et al., 2010; Stuart and Spruston, 2015; Beaulieu-Laroche et al., 2018; Poirazi and Papoutsi, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Dendrite structure has been successfully linked to connectivity and wiring requirements allowing the generation of highly realistic synthetic dendritic morphologies based on these principles alone.
source: Also, dendrite structure has been successfully linked to connectivity and wiring requirements allowing the generation of highly realistic synthetic dendritic morphologies based on these principles alone (Stepanyants et al., 2004; Wen and Chklovskii, 2008; Cuntz et al., 2010; Cuntz et al., 2007; Nanda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work.

claim: Efforts to link dendrite structure with computational tasks have fallen short of clarifying the link between the developmental elaboration of dendrite structure and the structural constraints dictated by the computational tasks of the neuron.
source: However, to date, these efforts have fallen short of clarifying the link between the developmental elaboration of dendrite structure and the structural constraints dictated by the computational tasks of the neuron (Lefebvre et al., 2015).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Unravelling dendrite patterning processes is important to achieve a mechanistic understanding of the nervous system and to gather insights into neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Unravelling these patterning processes is important to achieve a mechanistic understanding of the nervous system and to gather insights into neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders alike (Copf, 2016; Real et al., 2018; Forrest et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a motivational statement supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Drosophila is a genetically tractable animal model with existing comprehensive research in the fields of dendrite development, structure and function.
source: To attain an integrative view of dendrite functional assembly we decided to analyse a genetically tractable animal model, such as Drosophila, with existing comprehensive research in the fields of dendrite development, structure and function.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive citations to Drosophila research throughout the manuscript.

claim: Extensive investigations in the emergence of dendritic morphology and on the specific impact of dendritic morphology on computation make insects notably favourable to study mechanisms of development of dendrite form and function.
source: Extensive investigations in the emergence of dendritic morphology (Jan and Jan, 2010; Gerhard et al., 2017; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016; Enriquez et al., 2015; Corty et al., 2016; Ganguly et al., 2016; Nanda et al., 2018; Couton et al., 2015; Schlegel et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2020; Sheng et al., 2018) and on the specific impact of dendritic morphology on computation (Dewell and Gabbiani, 2017; Single and Borst, 1998; Gabbiani et al., 2002; Cuntz et al., 2003; Allen et al., 2006; Kohl et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017; Frechter et al., 2019; He et al., 2019) make insects notably favourable to study mechanisms of development of dendrite form and function.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research on insect dendrites.

claim: Four distinct classes of dendritic arborisation sensory neurons of the Drosophila larva peripheral nervous system are of particular interest because of the marked differences in their morphology and function.
source: A set of four distinct classes of dendritic arborisation sensory neurons of the Drosophila larva peripheral nervous system are of particular interest because of the marked differences in their morphology and function (Grueber et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grueber et al., 2002.

claim: The function of class I (c1da) proprioceptors is thought to tightly depend on dendritic morphology.
source: Among these cell types, the function of class I (c1da) proprioceptors is thought to tightly depend on dendritic morphology.
evidence: This is a statement based on prior knowledge and is supported by subsequent citations.

claim: c1da dendrites undergo sequential deformation in consecutive hemisegments by the contraction of the larva body wall during crawling.
source: In fact, c1da dendrites undergo sequential deformation in consecutive hemisegments by the contraction of the larva body wall during crawling (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heckscher et al., 2012.

claim: The structural deformation of c1da terminal branches coincides with c1da Ca2+ responses.
source: The structural deformation of c1da terminal branches coincides with c1da Ca2+ responses, an activation that could provide a possible propioceptive feedback to coordinate the peristaltic waves of muscle contractions (Hughes et al., 2007; Song et al., 2007; Vaadia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: c1da Ca2+ responses could provide a possible proprioceptive feedback to coordinate the peristaltic waves of muscle contractions.
source: The structural deformation of c1da terminal branches coincides with c1da Ca2+ responses, an activation that could provide a possible propioceptive feedback to coordinate the peristaltic waves of muscle contractions (Hughes et al., 2007; Song et al., 2007; Vaadia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Membrane curvature during branch deformation is thought to be directly linked to the opening of mechanically gated ion channels present in the c1da neuron membrane.
source: Membrane curvature during branch deformation is thought to be directly linked to the opening of mechanically gated ion channels present in the c1da neuron membrane (He et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to He et al., 2019.

claim: Genetic manipulation of c1da neuron morphology impaired the crawling behaviour.
source: These findings are supported by previous studies, where genetic manipulation of c1da neuron morphology (Hughes et al., 2007; Song et al., 2007) or null mutations of mechanosensitive channels expressed in the membrane of these sensory neurons (Cheng et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2016) impaired the crawling behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Null mutations of mechanosensitive channels expressed in the membrane of c1da sensory neurons impaired the crawling behaviour.
source: These findings are supported by previous studies, where genetic manipulation of c1da neuron morphology (Hughes et al., 2007; Song et al., 2007) or null mutations of mechanosensitive channels expressed in the membrane of these sensory neurons (Cheng et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2016) impaired the crawling behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: The relay of proprioceptive information about body movement is crucially dependent on the specific localisation of c1da neurons in the body segments, the association of their dendrites with the larval body wall and their precise dendritic morphology.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the relay of proprioceptive information about body movement is crucially dependent on the specific localisation of c1da neurons in the body segments, the association of their dendrites with the larval body wall and their precise dendritic morphology (Fushiki et al., 2016; Grueber et al., 2007; Vaadia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The dendrites of the ventral posterior c1da neuron (c1vpda) exhibit an unmistakable stereotypical comb-like shape with a main branch (MB) running perpendicularly to the anteroposterior direction of contraction and lateral branches typically running parallel to the direction of contraction.
source: In particular, the dendrites of the ventral posterior c1da neuron (c1vpda) exhibit an unmistakable stereotypical comb-like shape with a main branch (MB) running perpendicularly to the anteroposterior direction of contraction and lateral branches typically running parallel to the direction of contraction.
evidence: This is a morphological description supported by the imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: As the peristaltic muscle contraction wave progresses along the anteroposterior axis during crawling lateral branches bend, while the MB remains almost unaffected.
source: As the peristaltic muscle contraction wave progresses along the anteroposterior axis during crawling lateral branches bend, while the MB remains almost unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by the functional imaging data and prior work cited (Vaadia et al., 2019).

claim: The different deformation profiles of c1vpda branches likely arise from the distinct orientation of the branches.
source: The different deformation profiles likely arise from the distinct orientation of the branches (Vaadia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Vaadia et al., 2019.

claim: c1vpda neurons provide an ideal platform to address how dendrite structure is optimised towards the neuron's appropriate functional response and how such an optimised structure is achieved.
source: Dendrite morphology, dendrite activation pattern and function of c1vpda neurons are known. These sensory neurons thus provide an ideal platform to address how dendrite structure is optimised towards the neuron's appropriate functional response and such an optimised structure is achieved.
evidence: This is a rationale for the study based on existing knowledge.

claim: Analysis of the underlying developmental trajectories of distinct cell types provided important insights into how neurons and circuits pattern into functional structures.
source: In previous studies, analysis of the underlying developmental trajectories of distinct cell types provided important insights into how neurons (Miller, 1981; Lim et al., 2018) and circuits (Langen et al., 2015) pattern into functional structures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dendrite growth can to a large degree be described by a random growth process that satisfies optimal wire and a randomised retraction of branches that preferentially preserves functional dendrites.
source: We find that dendrite growth can to a large degree be described by a random growth process that satisfies optimal wire and a randomised retraction of branches that preferentially preserves functional dendrites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the computational modeling and experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The main branch (MB) emerged from the soma at around 16 hrs AEL and extended in a dorsal orientation.
source: Within the egg (Figure 1A), the main branch (MB) emerged from the soma at around 16 hrs AEL and extended in a dorsal orientation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A number of second-order lateral interstitial branches appeared from the initial MB extending in both the anterior and posterior directions.
source: Afterwards, a number of second-order lateral interstitial branches appeared from the initial MB extending in both the anterior and posterior directions, with the MB dorsal position potentially biasing their growth direction along the anteroposterior axis (Yoong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: The MB dorsal position potentially biases the growth direction of second-order lateral branches along the anteroposterior axis.
source: Afterwards, a number of second-order lateral interstitial branches appeared from the initial MB extending in both the anterior and posterior directions, with the MB dorsal position potentially biasing their growth direction along the anteroposterior axis (Yoong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Yoong et al., 2019.

claim: Shorter third-order lateral branches sprouted interstitially from the second-order lateral branches mainly along the dorsoventral axis.
source: Then, shorter third-order lateral branches sprouted interstitially from the second-order lateral branches mainly along the dorsoventral axis.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: Lateral branches underwent repeated cycles of extension and retraction until reaching a maximum number of branches around 18.5−19 hrs AEL.
source: Lateral branches underwent repeated cycles of extension and retraction until reaching a maximum number of branches around 18.5−19 hrs AEL.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 2B.

claim: Even at the stage of maximum branching, few fourth or fifth-order lateral branches were observed.
source: Even at this stage few fourth or fifth-order lateral branches were observed.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: The c1vpda sensory neuron entered a stage of arbour reorganisation marked predominantly by the retraction of branch tips.
source: The c1vpda sensory neuron then entered a stage of arbour reorganisation, marked predominantly by the retraction of branch tips (Figure 1A, 18.5 hrs and 19.5 hrs).
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: The retraction phase was followed by a pre-hatching stabilisation period.
source: This phase of removal of dendritic branches, hereafter referred as the retraction phase, was followed by a pre-hatching stabilisation period (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: During hatching, larvae showed severe head swings and anteroposterior contractions, followed by body swirls inside the egg preventing the collection of images in this period.
source: During hatching, larvae showed severe head swings and anteroposterior contractions, followed by body swirls inside the egg preventing the collection of images in this period.
evidence: This is an observational statement explaining a gap in the imaging data.

claim: After hatching, the neurons continued growing concomitantly with the expansion of the body wall.
source: After hatching (24 hrs AEL), we imaged dendrite development at the time points of 30 hrs, 50 hrs and 72 hrs AEL (Figure 1B). The neurons continued growing concomitantly with the expansion of the body wall.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: The post-embryonic growth phase preserved the shape and complexity of c1vpda dendrites, with only very few new branches emerging.
source: However, the post-embryonic growth phase preserved the shape and complexity of c1vpda dendrites, with only very few new branches emerging.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: The increase of dendrite cable during post-embryonic growth was due primarily to the scaling elongation of existing branches.
source: The increase of dendrite cable was due primarily to the scaling elongation of existing branches.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: The dendritic pattern observed at 30 hrs AEL was fundamentally the same as the one observed at 72 hrs AEL, consistent with an isometric scaling of da sensory neurons during larval stages.
source: The dendritic pattern observed at 30 hrs AEL was fundamentally the same as the one observed at 72 hrs AEL, consistent with an isometric scaling of da sensory neurons during larval stages (Parrish et al., 2009).
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1B and supported by a citation to Parrish et al., 2009.

claim: Developmental time was a strong source of variation in the morphological data with neurons becoming increasingly morphologically divergent over time.
source: After examining the tSNE plot, it is evident that developmental time was a strong source of variation in the data with neurons becoming increasingly morphologically divergent over time.
evidence: This is shown in the tSNE plot in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells from early stages formed large continuums in the tSNE plot, whereas darker green discrete clusters emerged at later stages (50−72 hrs AEL) due to dendrite morphological dissimilarity between the observation points.
source: Cells from early stages formed large continuums in the tSNE plot, whereas darker green discrete clusters emerged at later stages (50−72 hrs AEL) due to dendrite morphological dissimilarity between the observation points.
evidence: This is shown in the tSNE plot in Figure 2A.

claim: The non-linear developmental trajectory in the early embryonic stages reflects the intense dynamics of arbour outgrowth and refinement.
source: The non-linear developmental trajectory (yellow arrow) in the early embryonic stages reflects the intense dynamics of arbour outgrowth and refinement, while the subsequent more linear trajectory corresponds to the isometric stretching occurring in later stages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tSNE plot in Figure 2A.

claim: The subsequent more linear trajectory in the tSNE plot corresponds to the isometric stretching occurring in later stages.
source: The non-linear developmental trajectory (yellow arrow) in the early embryonic stages reflects the intense dynamics of arbour outgrowth and refinement, while the subsequent more linear trajectory corresponds to the isometric stretching occurring in later stages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tSNE plot in Figure 2A.

claim: Shorter, proximally located, higher-order lateral branches (third order or higher) were the ones most strongly involved in retraction.
source: This suggests that shorter, proximally located, higher-order lateral branches (third order or higher) were the ones most strongly involved in retraction (see also Figure 1A, arrows).
evidence: This is an inference from the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 1A.

claim: Higher-order lateral branches, due to their location in the inner part of the dendritic field, had only a small influence in defining the spanning area of the c1vpda dendrites.
source: These branches, due to their location in the inner part of the dendritic field had only a small influence in defining the spanning area of the c1vpda dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference from the morphological data.

claim: A square root relation between dendrite length L and surface area S, and a square root relation between total length L and number of branch points N were found at each developmental time point.
source: As predicted by the aforementioned equation, a square root relation between dendrite length L and surface area S, and a square root relation between total length L and number of branch points N were found at each developmental time point (Figure 2D; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and is consistent with the theoretical prediction.

claim: Throughout morphological differentiation during development, c1vpda sensory neurons respect minimum wire constraints.
source: Taken together, the results indicate that throughout morphological differentiation during development, c1vpda sensory neurons respect minimum wire constraints.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scaling analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: While functional requirements for dendritic morphology may shape the dendrites, these must also respect wire optimisation constraints.
source: This suggests that while functional requirements for dendritic morphology here may shape the dendrites, these must also respect wire optimisation constraints.
evidence: This is an inference from the wire optimization analysis.

claim: Smaller, dorsoventral oriented, higher-order lateral branches were preferentially eliminated in the embryonic retraction phase, leaving most second-order lateral branches intact.
source: The time series of c1vpda growth in Figure 1A suggested that smaller, dorsoventral oriented, higher-order lateral branches were preferentially eliminated in the embryonic retraction phase, leaving most second-order lateral branches intact.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: The innervation of the anteroposterior axis by post-embryonic c1vpda second-order lateral branches may play a role in sampling cuticle folding during crawling behaviour.
source: This is interesting, as the innervation of the anteroposterior axis by post-embryonic c1vpda second-order lateral branches may play a role in sampling cuticle folding during crawling behaviour (Vaadia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Vaadia et al., 2019.

claim: The median branch lengths and angles of second-order lateral branches (6.1 µm and 63.93°) and higher-order lateral branches (2 µm and 41.67°) remained similar after retraction.
source: Interestingly, the median branch lengths and angles of second-order lateral branches (6.1 µm and 63.93°) and higher-order lateral branches (2 µm and 41.67°) remained similar after retraction (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with quantitative measurements.

claim: A drastic reduction in the overall number of branches was asymmetrically distributed between the different branch orders.
source: However, a drastic reduction in the overall number of branches was asymmetrically distributed between the different branch orders.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 comparing before and after retraction.

claim: The reduction of higher-order lateral branches (267 branches before retraction vs. 92 branches after retraction, with a decrease of −64.9%) greatly exceeded the reduction of second-order lateral branches (162 branches before retraction vs. 131 branches after retraction, with a decrease of −19.1%).
source: The reduction of higher-order lateral branches (267 branches before retraction vs. 92 branches after retraction, with a decrease of −64.9%) greatly exceeded the reduction of second-order lateral branches (162 branches before retraction vs. 131 branches after retraction, with a decrease of −19.1%).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 with quantitative measurements.

claim: The retraction stage reshaped the overall branch angle distributions towards higher angles, that is, further oriented along the anteroposterior axis.
source: Importantly, the retraction stage seemed to reshape the overall branch angle distributions towards higher angles, that is, further oriented along the anteroposterior axis (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 comparing angle distributions before and after retraction.

claim: The integration of mechanical cues by c1da sensory neurons through activation of mechanogated ion channels depends on the curvature of individual dendritic branches.
source: A recent study proposed that the integration of mechanical cues by c1da sensory neurons through activation of mechanogated ion channels depends on the curvature of individual dendritic branches (He et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to He et al., 2019.

claim: It remains unclear whether c1da dendritic branches are spatially arranged to maximise mechanical cue transduction through curvature.
source: However, it remains unclear whether c1da dendritic branches are spatially arranged to maximise mechanical cue transduction through curvature.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Ca2+ signals decreased as the peristaltic wave advanced to adjacent anterior segments.
source: Ca2+ signals decreased as the peristaltic wave advanced to adjacent anterior segments (see Figure 4—videos 1–3).
evidence: This is shown in the videos referenced in Figure 4.

claim: c1vpda sensory neurons respond to body wall folding during segment contraction with prominent Ca2+ signals in the dendrites.
source: These data replicate the results previously found by Vaadia et al., 2019, supporting the finding that c1vpda sensory neurons respond to body wall folding during segment contraction with prominent Ca2+ signals in the dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4A and a citation to Vaadia et al., 2019.

claim: Branch curvature increased steadily with the increase of the respective orientation angle independently of branch length or the size of the cylinder.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, branch curvature increased steadily with the increase of the respective orientation angle independently of branch length or the size of the cylinder.
evidence: This is shown in the modeling results in Figure 4B.

claim: Dendritic branches extending along the anteroposterior body axis may be in the optimal orientation for bending during segment contraction.
source: Our data and modelling indicate that dendritic branches extending along the anteroposterior body axis may be in the optimal orientation for bending during segment contraction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling and data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The increment in bending curvature was caused by the retraction of low bending curvature branches.
source: The increment was caused by the retraction of low bending curvature branches (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Functional constraints of mechanical responsiveness may represent a strong determinant in c1vpda dendrites patterning.
source: Taken together, these data and simulations suggest that functional constraints of mechanical responsiveness may represent a strong determinant in c1vpda dendrites patterning.
evidence: This is an inference from the curvature analysis and functional imaging data.

claim: The random retraction was the only scheme that yielded good results across all morphometrics compared to the experimental data.
source: Surprisingly, the random retraction was the only scheme that yielded good results across all morphometrics compared to the experimental data.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 comparing different retraction schemes.

claim: Random retraction of branches is a potential candidate to explain the biological data.
source: Our simulations exclude the more extreme versions of some possible retraction schemes while identifying a random retraction of branches as a potential candidate to explain the biological data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the retraction simulations in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Random retraction could be responsible for developing the c1vpda comb-like shape in a self-organised manner that may be less costly to genetically encode than a deterministic retraction program.
source: This type of random retraction could be responsible for developing the c1vpda comb-like shape in a self-organised manner that may be less costly to genetically encode than a deterministic retraction program (Hiesinger and Hassan, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Hiesinger and Hassan, 2018.

claim: Random retraction would make the scheme efficient at realising functionally specialised morphologies while being itself potentially the product of a rather non-specialised genetic program.
source: Interestingly, this would make the random retraction scheme efficient at realising functionally specialised morphologies while being itself potentially the product of a rather non-specialised genetic program.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the modeling results.

claim: The results suggest a branch type and time invariant mechanism of branch extension and reduction in c1vpda sensory neurons.
source: This analysis suggests a branch type and time invariant mechanism of branch extension and reduction in c1vpda sensory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference from the branch tracking data in Figure 5B.

claim: The specific proportion of branches per branch type must vary across the examined development window in order to accommodate a retraction phase.
source: Since the rates of extension and reduction were similar throughout, the specific proportion of branches per branch type must vary across the examined development window in order to accommodate a retraction phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the branch tracking data in Figure 5B.

claim: An initial phase of more intense branch dynamics, with only a small amount of branches remaining stable, lasted approximately half of the analysed time period.
source: Indeed, an initial phase of more intense branch dynamics, with only a small amount of branches remaining stable, lasted approximately half of the analysed time period.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the initial phase of branch dynamics, roughly half of the branches were involved in retraction while the number of new and elongating branches decreased steadily over time.
source: In that period of time, roughly half of the branches were involved in retraction while the number of new and elongating branches decreased steadily over time (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The initial phase of branch dynamics was followed by a phase defined by the sharp decrease in the number of retracting branches, contrasting with the increase of stable branches, corresponding to the initiation of the stabilisation stage.
source: This was followed by a phase defined by the sharp decrease in the number of retracting branches, contrasting with the increase of stable branches, corresponding to the initiation of the stabilisation stage.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the stabilisation phase, the number of new branches kept decreasing to virtually negligible values.
source: In this latter phase, the number of new branches kept decreasing to virtually negligible values.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the stabilisation phase, the proportion of elongating branches increased back to efficiently compensate for the remaining shortening further contributing to the stabilisation phase.
source: In the same time, the proportion of elongating branches increased back to efficiently compensate for the remaining shortening further contributing to the stabilisation phase.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both retraction simulations and measurements of single branch dynamics indicate that retraction is neither specific to functionally suboptimal branches, nor to smaller or higher-order branches but stochastic in nature.
source: In conclusion, both our retraction simulations as well as measurements of single branch dynamics indicate that retraction is neither specific to functionally suboptimal branches, nor to smaller or higher-order branches but stochastic in nature.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the retraction simulations and branch tracking data.

claim: The stochasticity of retraction does not prevent it from supporting optimal mechanical responsiveness.
source: Nevertheless, the stochasticity of retraction does not prevent it from supporting optimal mechanical responsiveness as shown above.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined results of stochastic retraction and functional optimization.

claim: The c1vpda growth model reproduces the patterning of real neurons by simulating branch dynamics on a synthetic dendritic tree at a given time point to produce the tree in the following time point.
source: The c1vpda growth model reproduces the patterning of real neurons by simulating branch dynamics on a synthetic dendritic tree at a given time point to produce the tree in the following time point.
evidence: This describes the computational model presented in Figure 6.

claim: The number of branch points, total length and surface area were consistently well fitted by the growth model with random retraction at all simulated developmental stages.
source: The number of branch points, total length and surface area were consistently well fitted by the growth model with random retraction at all simulated developmental stages (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model reproduced the scaling relationships from Figure 2D, indicating that the morphologies resulting from the random retraction growth model followed basic wire constraints as observed in the real data.
source: Importantly, the model reproduced the scaling relationships from Figure 2D, indicating that the morphologies resulting from the random retraction growth model followed basic wire constraints as observed in the real data (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The model strengthened the hypothesis that a stochastic retraction was responsible for arbour refinement in c1vpda sensory neurons.
source: The model strengthened the hypothesis that a stochastic retraction was responsible for arbour refinement in c1vpda sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: The model branch length and angle distributions before and after retraction matched the real data.
source: The model branch length and angle distributions before and after retraction matched the real data (Figure 6D, Figure 3) as well as the selective retraction of lower curvature branches observed in Figure 4 (lower curvature branches ranging between 0−0.2 retraction = −70% vs. higher curvature branches ranging between 1−0.8 retraction = −37.64%; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D compared to Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: A stochastic growth that satisfies wire constraints combined with random retraction of terminals are consistent with c1vpda dendrite morphogenesis and refinement.
source: All together, these findings indicate that a stochastic growth that satisfies wire constraints combined with random retraction of terminals are consistent with c1vpda dendrite morphogenesis and refinement.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: The lateral branches from the model slightly under-estimated the orientation angle of the second-order lateral branches after retraction (median model = 60.18° vs. median real neurons = 63.93°).
source: However, although the random retraction model successfully reproduced the most significant morphometrics of the experimental data, we note that the lateral branches from the model slightly under-estimated the orientation angle of the second-order lateral branches after retraction (median model = 60.18° vs. median real neurons = 63.93°).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between model and data.

claim: Other mechanisms may be involved in enhancing tips growth direction preference, such as specific cell adhesion molecules.
source: This indicates that possibly other mechanisms may be involved in enhancing tips growth direction preference, such as specific cell adhesion molecules (Hattori et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Hattori et al., 2013.

claim: The spatiotemporal patterning of c1vpda mechanosensory dendrites during development can be accurately predicted by a noisy growth model that conserves wire, in combination with a stochastic retraction that plausibly enhances their performance at sensing larval contractions.
source: We have shown that the spatiotemporal patterning of c1vpda mechanosensory dendrites during development can be accurately predicted by a noisy growth model that conserves wire, in combination with a stochastic retraction that plausibly enhances their performance at sensing larval contractions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: A sequence of three simple stages (1) MB polarisation, (2) subsequent branch outgrowth and (3) a final stochastic retraction stage generates specialised dendrites that favour functional branches, as found in real c1vpda sensory neurons.
source: We showed how a sequence of three simple stages (1) MB polarisation, (2) subsequent branch outgrowth and (3) a final stochastic retraction stage generates specialised dendrites that favour functional branches, as found in real c1vpda sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the developmental process described in the study.

claim: C1vpda development started with the polarisation of the MB.
source: C1vpda development started with the polarisation of the MB.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the data in Figure 1.

claim: The growth direction of the MB was constant across cells, with the MB of neurons from different hemisegments projecting dorsally, parallel to each other.
source: The growth direction of the MB was constant across cells, with the MB of neurons from different hemisegments projecting dorsally, parallel to each other (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1.

claim: During the extension phase, newly formed lateral branches emerged interstitially from the existing MB.
source: During the subsequent extension phase, newly formed lateral branches emerged interstitially from the existing MB.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the data in Figure 1.

claim: A multistage developmental program that incorporates stochastic processes can generate stereotypical phenotypical outcomes.
source: Prior work in neuronal circuit wiring showed how a multistage developmental program that incorporates stochastic processes can generate stereotypical phenotypical outcomes (Langen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Langen et al., 2015.

claim: Molecular mechanisms that utilise stochasticity can implement simple patterning rules.
source: This counterintuitive phenomenon is made possible in part by molecular mechanisms that utilise stochasticity to implement simple patterning rules (Hiesinger and Hassan, 2018; Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Johnston and Desplan, 2010; Courgeon and Desplan, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For c1vpda neurons, a combination of MB orientation, noisy filopodial exploration and contact-based local decisions on where to grow using Dscam based self-avoidance synergised to coordinate lateral branch patterning.
source: Arguably for the case of c1vpda neurons, a combination of MB orientation, noisy filopodial exploration and contact-based local decisions on where to grow using Dscam based self-avoidance synergised to coordinate lateral branch patterning (Grueber et al., 2003a; Zipursky and Grueber, 2013; Matthews et al., 2007; Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Soba et al., 2007; Dong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The initial innervation of the dendrite's spanning field by lateral branches produced optimally wired and space-filling dendrites.
source: The initial innervation of the dendrite's spanning field by lateral branches produced – similarly to previously observed class IV da neurons – optimally wired (see Figure 2) and space-filling dendrites (Baltruschat et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2 and a citation to Baltruschat et al., 2020.

claim: In the c1vpda the branches at the early stage divided into two distinct morphological classes: (1) longer second-order lateral branches that spread along the anteroposterior axis with growing tips mostly targeting distal and sparser areas of the dendritic territory, and (2) shorter higher-order lateral branches that mainly innervated the dorsoventral axis, and were more often located in proximal and densely packed areas of the dendrite's spanning field.
source: In the c1vpda the branches at this early stage divided into two distinct morphological classes: (1) longer second-order lateral branches that spread along the anteroposterior axis with growing tips mostly targeting distal and sparser areas of the dendritic territory. (2) In contrast, higher-order lateral branches exhibited shorter lengths, mainly innervating the dorsoventral axis, and more often located in proximal and densely packed areas of the dendrite's spanning field.
evidence: This is a morphological description supported by the data in Figure 3.

claim: Studies based on low temporal resolution static data of dendrite development suggested that distinct growth and retraction phases may happen sequentially during development.
source: In the past, studies based on low temporal resolution static data of dendrite development suggested that distinct growth and retraction phases may happen sequentially during development (Lázár, 1973; Huttenlocher and Dabholkar, 1997; Bystron et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: At higher temporal resolution, time-lapse movies showed that branch additions and retractions seem to happen rather concurrently during arbour elaboration.
source: At higher temporal resolution, time-lapse movies showed that branch additions and retractions seem to happen rather concurrently during arbour elaboration (Hua and Smith, 2004; Hossain et al., 2012; Cline, 2001; Dailey and Smith, 1996; Yoong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the c1vpda dataset, parallel growth and retraction of branches with changes in their proportions led to separate phases of predominant outgrowth, retraction and then stabilisation.
source: In our dataset on c1vpda, we observed parallel growth and retraction of branches with changes in their proportions leading to separate phases of predominant outgrowth, retraction and then stabilisation.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 1, 2, and 5.

claim: The retraction of a dendritic tree could have economical purposes and minimise the amount of wire, or it could refine the branching pattern to enhance functionality.
source: The retraction of a dendritic tree could have economical purposes and minimise the amount of wire, or it could refine the branching pattern to enhance functionality.
evidence: This presents two possible interpretations of retraction.

claim: The data indicate that retraction refines the branching pattern to enhance functionality rather than minimising wire.
source: Our data indicate that the latter is the case, with a simple random retraction selectively remodelling the tree structure, influencing the mechanisms of dendritic signal integration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the retraction simulations in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The biased retraction of higher-order lateral branches was attained due to the combination of three factors: asymmetry of branch length distributions between branch orders, branch reduction and extension rates similarity and invariance in time and across branch orders, and the increase of the proportion of branch reductions during the retraction phase.
source: However, the biased retraction of higher-order lateral branches was really attained due to the combination of three factors: asymmetry of branch length distributions between branch orders (Figure 3), branch reduction and extension rates similarity and invariance in time and across branch orders, and the increase of the proportion of branch reductions during the retraction phase (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism of biased retraction supported by data in Figures 3 and 5B.

claim: The random selection of a large number of branches to retract a constant amount of cable from their tips led to the penalisation of higher-order lateral branches due to their smaller lengths.
source: Taken together, the random selection of a large number of branches to retract a constant amount of cable from their tips led to the penalisation of higher-order lateral branches due to their smaller lengths.
evidence: This is an inference from the branch tracking and retraction simulation data.

claim: Second-order lateral branches characterised by longer lengths retracted less.
source: In contrast, second-order lateral branches characterised by longer lengths retracted less.
evidence: This is an inference from the branch tracking and retraction simulation data.

claim: A genetically determined mechanism could cause the observed stochastic retraction at a stereotypical developmental time.
source: The first possibility is that a genetically determined mechanism would cause the observed stochastic retraction at a stereotypical developmental time.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The retraction period could be activity-dependent.
source: We speculate as well that the retraction period could be activity-dependent.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Activity coordinates the development of functional neurons in visual and motor systems of Drosophila.
source: It has been demonstrated that activity coordinates the development of functional neurons in visual and motor systems of Drosophila (Fushiki et al., 2013; Akin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The observed peristaltic waves during embryonic stages could potentially activate c1vpda cells and signal the beginning of the retraction phase and subsequent cell maturation.
source: For the case of c1vpda neurons, the observed peristaltic waves during embryonic stages could potentially activate these cells and signal the beginning of the retraction phase and subsequent cell maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility discussed in the manuscript.

claim: As the number of dendrite branches and cable increase during the extension phase competition-based mechanisms could provide adaptive negative feedback on branch growth, to avoid uncontrolled innervation.
source: Alternatively, as the number of dendrite branches and cable increase during the extension phase competition-based mechanisms could provide adaptive negative feedback on branch growth, to avoid uncontrolled innervation.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Competition-based mechanisms may result from different levels of intrinsic stabilisation in the different types of branches that could lead to the elimination of the smaller branches and weakly supported tips, or branches contacting in densely packed areas of the dendritic field could drive tips to mutually retract.
source: These mechanisms may either result from different levels of intrinsic stabilisation in the different types of branches that could lead to the elimination of the smaller branches and weakly supported tips, or branches contacting in densely packed areas of the dendritic field could drive tips to mutually retract (Palavalli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative possibility supported by a citation to Palavalli et al., 2020.

claim: Dscam based molecular machinery may help implementing a developmental program computationally equivalent to minimum spanning tree algorithms.
source: The latter hypothesis potentially involving Dscam is of particular interest since we proposed previously that Dscam based molecular machinery may help implementing a developmental program computationally equivalent to minimum spanning tree algorithms (Cuntz et al., 2010; Cuntz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: After the retraction step, c1vpda trees went through a stabilisation period, characterised by a negligible increase in cable length, surface area, and number of branches through a net balance of shortening and elongation of branches.
source: After the retraction step, c1vpda trees went through a stabilisation period, characterised by a negligible increase in cable length, surface area, and number of branches through a net balance of shortening and elongation of branches (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1.

claim: After hatching, the dendrites experienced an isometric scaling, where the comb-like pattern and branching complexity of the dendrites persisted across all larval stages, and the cable and surface were increased following the larva's body growth.
source: After hatching, the dendrites experienced an isometric scaling, where the comb-like pattern and branching complexity of the dendrites persisted across all larval stages, and the cable and surface were increased following the larva's body growth (Parrish et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1B and a citation to Parrish et al., 2009.

claim: The conservation of dendrite shape throughout larval stages suggests the need for functional conservation during larval development.
source: The conservation of dendrite shape throughout larval stages suggests the need for functional conservation during larval development.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of isometric scaling.

claim: The behavioural repertoire of L1 larvae was analogous to L3 larvae.
source: This observation is consistent with previously reported results, that showed that the behavioural repertoire of L1 larvae was analogous to L3 larvae (Almeida-Carvalho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Almeida-Carvalho et al., 2017.

claim: Besides fulfilling their functional role, c1vpda neurons also optimise resources.
source: However, besides fulfilling their functional role, c1vpda neurons also optimise resources.
evidence: This is supported by the wire optimization analysis in Figure 2.

claim: The overproduction of material carries a fitness cost to the organism and as a result a trade-off between function and resources conservation arises.
source: The overproduction of material carries a fitness cost to the organism and as a result a trade-off between function and resources conservation arises (Szekely et al., 2013; Wen and Chklovskii, 2008; Cuntz et al., 2007; Bullmore and Sporns, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A noisy growth process with different stages optimises function, structure and wire in a self-organised manner.
source: Here, we showed that a noisy growth process with different stages optimises function, structure and wire in a self-organised manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: A variety of models have been proposed to generate neuronal morphologies reproducing morphometrics of real mature dendrites.
source: In the past, a variety of models have been proposed to generate neuronal morphologies reproducing morphometrics of real mature dendrites (Cuntz et al., 2007; Cuntz et al., 2010; Donohue and Ascoli, 2008; Eberhard et al., 2006; Koene et al., 2009; Torben-Nielsen and De Schutter, 2014; Luczak, 2006; Beining et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Some growth models rely on large number of parameters that are not available from experimental data, and they tend to provide phenomenological insights rather than a mechanistic understanding of a given system.
source: However, some of these growth models rely on large number of parameters that are not available from experimental data, and they tend to provide phenomenological insights rather than a mechanistic understanding of a given system (Goodhill, 2018).
evidence: This is a critique of prior modeling approaches supported by a citation to Goodhill, 2018.

claim: None of the prior modeling approaches have specifically modelled development quantitatively.
source: Most notably, none of those approaches have specifically modelled development quantitatively (but see Yalgin et al., 2015; Sugimura et al., 2007; Baltruschat et al., 2020).
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior modeling work, with some exceptions cited.

claim: None of the prior modeling approaches have focused on a quantitative understanding of retraction in the developmental process even though the importance has been emphasised widely.
source: Also none of those approaches have focused on a quantitative understanding of retraction in the developmental process even though the importance has been emphasised widely (van Pelt, 1997; Beining et al., 2017; Luczak, 2006; Torben-Nielsen and De Schutter, 2014; Williams and Truman, 2004).
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior modeling work, supported by citations.

claim: The chosen temporal resolution for imaging was determined as a trade-off between capturing c1vpda dendrite dynamics throughout embryonic and larval stages and tracing speed.
source: Due to the lack of high-throughput automatic digital tracing algorithms for neuronal morphologies the chosen temporal resolution for imaging (see Materials and methods) was determined as a trade-off between capturing c1vpda dendrite dynamics throughout embryonic and larval stages and tracing speed (Helmstaedter, 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation to Helmstaedter, 2013.

claim: Branch dynamics and morphometrics at the chosen temporal resolution were well defined by a stochastic growth and retraction model, suggesting that c1vpda morphogenesis is possibly a non-deterministic process.
source: Branch dynamics and morphometrics at this stage were well defined by a stochastic growth and retraction model, suggesting that c1vpda morphogenesis is possibly a non-deterministic process, in accordance with other previously found results for other cell types (Ryglewski et al., 2017; Özel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results and citations to prior research.

claim: The accordance between data and model further validates the chosen temporal resolution of imaging.
source: The accordance between data and model further validates the chosen temporal resolution of imaging.
evidence: This is an inference from the good fit between model and data.

claim: As more sophisticated tracing algorithms develop, more detailed datasets will become available for analysis and modelling.
source: In the future, as more sophisticated tracing algorithms develop, more detailed datasets will become available for analysis and modelling (Peng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2017.

claim: The stereotypical comb-like shaped c1vpda dendrites optimally sense the mechanical strain due to the hinge-like dynamics during cuticle folding.
source: It was previously suggested that the stereotypical comb-like shaped c1vpda dendrites optimally sense the mechanical strain due to the hinge-like dynamics during cuticle folding (Vaadia et al., 2019; He et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vaadia et al., 2019 and He et al., 2019.

claim: Theoretical results on elastic properties of lipid bilayers showed that curvature is dependent on the orientation of the membrane.
source: Interestingly, previous theoretical results on elastic properties of lipid bilayers showed that curvature is dependent on the orientation of the membrane (Helfrich, 1973; Bahrami et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The second-order lateral branches are better suited for mechanical sensory cues transduction arising from cuticle folding during crawling behaviour than higher-order lateral branches.
source: Based on theoretical predictions (Figure 4), we propose that the second-order lateral branches are better suited for mechanical sensory cues transduction arising from cuticle folding during crawling behaviour than higher-order lateral branches.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the modeling results in Figure 4.

claim: Due to their direction preference running along the anteroposterior axis second-order lateral branches experience larger curvature increase, possibly increasing the opening probability of the mechanogated ion channels.
source: Due to their direction preference running along the anteroposterior axis these branches experience larger curvature increase, possibly increasing the opening probability of the mechanogated ion channels (Liang and Howard, 2018; Katta et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results supported by citations to prior research on mechanogated ion channels.

claim: Similar sensory neurons (dorsal c1da mechanosensory neurons c1ddaE and c1ddaD) may become activated by membrane curvature increase.
source: These results strengthen a recently proposed hypothesis, which predicted that similar sensory neurons (dorsal c1da mechanosensory neurons c1ddaE and c1ddaD) may become activated by membrane curvature increase (He et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to He et al., 2019.

claim: C1da neurons contain denser arrays of microtubules in their branches than other da classes, and are firmly anchored to the epithelium by pads of electron dense material.
source: C1da neurons contain denser arrays of microtubules in their branches than other da classes, and are firmly anchored to the epithelium by pads of electron dense material (Delandre et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Delandre et al., 2016.

claim: Structural adaptations in the microtubule mesh of c1da sensory neurons support their role in sensing and responding to mechanical stimuli arising from the contraction of the body wall.
source: Several findings are consistent with this hypothesis. Unique structural adaptations in the microtubule mesh of c1da sensory neurons support their role in sensing and responding to mechanical stimuli arising from the contraction of the body wall.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observations.

claim: Structural adaptations in c1da neurons are also present in other cells active in mechanotransduction.
source: These structural adaptations are also present in other cells active in mechanotransduction (Krieg et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Similar results were reported in C. elegans, suggesting that dendrite curvature may provide the biophysical substrate of mechanosensory experience across multiple animal models.
source: Moreover, similar results were reported in C. elegans, suggesting that dendrite curvature may provide the biophysical substrate of mechanosensory experience across multiple animal models (Albeg et al., 2011; Hall and Treinin, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research in C. elegans.

claim: A specialised dendritic tree pattern that minimises wire can be obtained by the precise temporal arrangement of stochastic developmental programs.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that a specialised dendritic tree pattern that minimises wire can be obtained by the precise temporal arrangement of stochastic developmental programs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Evidence can be found that similar stages and strategies may be preserved across different cell types and species.
source: Interestingly, evidence can be found that similar stages and strategies may be preserved across different cell types (Richardson and Shen, 2019; Gao et al., 2000; Sugimura et al., 2003; Baltruschat et al., 2020) and species (Yoong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The flexible usage of self-organisational programs provides developmental resilience and robustness to perturbations in the growth medium.
source: The flexible usage of such self-organisational programs provides developmental resilience and robustness to perturbations in the growth medium (Hiesinger and Hassan, 2018; Johnston and Desplan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-organisational programs possibly avoid the encoding of a deterministic morphogenetic program that may be more costly to implement genetically.
source: It also possibly avoids the encoding of a deterministic morphogenetic program that may be more costly to implement genetically (Hiesinger and Hassan, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Hiesinger and Hassan, 2018.

claim: It will be interesting to elucidate the mechanisms that control the temporal sequence of distinct stages of branch elaboration for the c1vpda sensory neurons.
source: In the future, it will be interesting to elucidate the mechanisms that control the temporal sequence of distinct stages of branch elaboration for the c1vpda sensory neurons (Grueber et al., 2003a; Jinushi-Nakao et al., 2007; Nanda et al., 2019) and on a higher scale to understand to what extent similar self-organising processes and mechanisms are implicated in the formation of other cell types (Ryglewski et al., 2017; Özel et al., 2015), neuronal networks (Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015) and even in the emergence of non-neuronal branching organs (Hannezo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement supported by citations to relevant literature.
